frames.narration: A team submits a training job that needs 256 GPUs, which is 32 nodes of 8. The request carries the team, a priority and a maximum run time of 12 hours. It is stored in the durable queue, so a scheduler restart cannot lose it.
The scheduler reads the team's usage from the quota ledger. The team is below its fair share, so the job is near the front of the queue. If it were above its share, other teams would go first.

Rack 7 has 32 completely empty nodes, exactly 256 GPUs in one rack. The scheduler reserves all of them in one step. If even one node were missing, it would reserve nothing and let shorter jobs backfill while it waits.

The scheduler tells the node agents to start one worker on each of the 32 nodes. The workers find each other, load the last checkpoint if there is one, and the job counts as running only when all 256 have joined.

While it trains, the job writes a checkpoint every 30 minutes. For a 70-billion-parameter model at 14 bytes per parameter, a checkpoint is about 980 GB, which the shared storage absorbs in a few seconds.

Hours later one GPU reports memory errors and a worker stops responding. The agents' heartbeats and the job's own timeout both show it, and the health service cordons the bad node so nothing new will be placed there.

The gang is released. Rack 7 has 31 healthy nodes, so the scheduler takes a spare node from rack 9, which costs a little speed for crossing racks but is better than waiting for a repair. It asks for 256 GPUs again and the job resumes from the last checkpoint, with at most 30 minutes of work lost.

The team sees the job back at work, and the scheduler records the run: queue time, GPU-hours used and the hours lost to the failure. The numbers feed per-team usage, so the next fair-share decision accounts for them.
